name: the Tiergarten
title: Ancient Trees in Berlin's Tiergarten, Oldest First
meta_description: Berlin's old hunting forest was cut for firewood after 1945. A sequoia planted in 1891 came through, and the zoo claims 500 years for its oak.
intro:
The Tiergarten began in the sixteenth century as the Electors' hunting forest, and the oldest age anyone claims for a tree in it is 500 years, Berlin Zoo's word for a pedunculate oak in its grounds. That is the owner's figure, not a measurement. Most of what stands here is younger, for a hard reason: in the hungry winters after 1945 Berliners cut most of the park down for firewood, and it was replanted from 1949.

A giant sequoia planted in 1891 near Schloss Bellevue came through. Queen Elizabeth II added a red oak by the Teehaus in 1965, on her first visit to West Berlin. Around them, Berlin protects trees as natural monuments, many of them listed on a single day, 2 March 1993, and the register says why: beauty alone for the tulip tree on the Luiseninsel, rarity for a Lebanon oak from the mountains of the Near East, and four reasons at once, science among them, for a sessile oak by the Carillon. A black locust grows on the traffic island under the Victory Column, reached through the pedestrian tunnels.

Almost none of them has a published age or girth, so a tape measure is a fair thing to bring. The park is free and open at all hours; the zoo oak needs a ticket.
